Example 1

This example takes an IP address from a user, verifies that it is well formed and then looks up the hostname and copies it into a buffer.




(bad code)

Example Language: C 
                                    
                                


void host_lookup(char *user_supplied_addr){
struct hostent *hp;in_addr_t *addr;char hostname[64];in_addr_t inet_addr(const char *cp);

/*routine that ensures user_supplied_addr is in the right format for conversion */

validate_addr_form(user_supplied_addr);addr = inet_addr(user_supplied_addr);hp = gethostbyaddr( addr, sizeof(struct in_addr), AF_INET);strcpy(hostname, hp->h_name);
}




This function allocates a buffer of 64 bytes to store the hostname, however there is no guarantee that the hostname will not be larger than 64 bytes. If an attacker specifies an address which resolves to a very large hostname, then the function may overwrite sensitive data or even relinquish control flow to the attacker.
Note that this example also contains an unchecked return value (CWE-252) that can lead to a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476).



Example 2

This example applies an encoding procedure to an input string and stores it into a buffer.




(bad code)

Example Language: C 
                                    
                                


char * copy_input(char *user_supplied_string){
int i, dst_index;char *dst_buf = (char*)malloc(4*sizeof(char) * MAX_SIZE);if ( MAX_SIZE <= strlen(user_supplied_string) ){die("user string too long, die evil hacker!");}dst_index = 0;for ( i = 0; i < strlen(user_supplied_string); i++ ){
if( '&' == user_supplied_string[i] ){dst_buf[dst_index++] = '&';dst_buf[dst_index++] = 'a';dst_buf[dst_index++] = 'm';dst_buf[dst_index++] = 'p';dst_buf[dst_index++] = ';';}else if ('<' == user_supplied_string[i] ){
/* encode to < */

}else dst_buf[dst_index++] = user_supplied_string[i];
}return dst_buf;
}




The programmer attempts to encode the ampersand character in the user-controlled string, however the length of the string is validated before the encoding procedure is applied. Furthermore, the programmer assumes encoding expansion will only expand a given character by a factor of 4, while the encoding of the ampersand expands by 5. As a result, when the encoding procedure expands the string it is possible to overflow the destination buffer if the attacker provides a string of many ampersands.



Example 3

The following example asks a user for an offset into an array to select an item.




(bad code)

Example Language: C 
                                    
                                



int main (int argc, char **argv) {char *items[] = {"boat", "car", "truck", "train"};int index = GetUntrustedOffset();printf("You selected %s\n", items[index-1]);}




The programmer allows the user to specify which element in the list to select, however an attacker can provide an out-of-bounds offset, resulting in a buffer over-read (CWE-126).



Example 4

In the following code, the method retrieves a value from an array at a specific array index location that is given as an input parameter to the method




(bad code)

Example Language: C 
                                    
                                


int getValueFromArray(int *array, int len, int index) {

int value;

// check that the array index is less than the maximum


// length of the array
if (index < len) {

// get the value at the specified index of the array
value = array[index];
}
// if array index is invalid then output error message

// and return value indicating error
else {printf("Value is: %d\n", array[index]);value = -1;}
return value;
}




However, this method only verifies that the given array index is less than the maximum length of the array but does not check for the minimum value (CWE-839). This will allow a negative value to be accepted as the input array index, which will result in a out of bounds read (CWE-125) and may allow access to sensitive memory. The input array index should be checked to verify that is within the maximum and minimum range required for the array (CWE-129). In this example the if statement should be modified to include a minimum range check, as shown below.




(good code)

Example Language: C 
                                    
                                



...

// check that the array index is within the correct


// range of values for the array
if (index >= 0 && index < len) {
...







Example 5

Windows provides the _mbs family of functions to perform various operations on multibyte strings. When these functions are passed a malformed multibyte string, such as a string containing a valid leading byte followed by a single null byte, they can read or write past the end of the string buffer causing a buffer overflow. The following functions all pose a risk of buffer overflow: _mbsinc _mbsdec _mbsncat _mbsncpy _mbsnextc _mbsnset _mbsrev _mbsset _mbsstr _mbstok _mbccpy _mbslen
metadata.functionality:
Functionality:  

Accept user input from the console, convert it to bytes, copy it into a fixed-size buffer, and then display the contents of the buffer as a string.
metadata.root_cause: KeyConcept: [Buffer overflow vulnerabilities occur when data from an external source, such as user input, is copied into a fixed-size memory buffer without verifying that the data size does not exceed the buffer's capacity. If the input data surpasses the buffer's allocated space, the copying process can overwrite adjacent memory regions, leading to unpredictable behavior, program crashes, or security exploits. This typically happens when the length of the source data is used directly in copy or write operations without proper validation or bounds checking, resulting in potential memory corruption.]

page_content:
**Functionality:**  
Populate an integer array with multiples of ten based on their indices, aiming to assign values sequentially from zero upward.

KeyConcept:ArrayBoundaryCheckFailure [A vulnerability arising from failure to enforce correct boundary conditions during array iteration leads to attempts to access indices outside of valid array bounds. Arrays in most programming languages are zero-indexed, meaning valid indices range from zero up to (length - 1). When iteration logic uses a comparison operator that allows the index to reach the array's length, an out-of-bounds access occurs, resulting in runtime errors or undefined behavior. Such violations can cause application crashes, data corruption, or security risks if exploited. Proper boundary conditions—typically using the less-than operator—must be enforced to ensure iteration stays within valid index ranges, preserving stability and preventing vulnerabilities.]

Vulnerability Report for BufferOverflowExample3.java

---

**1) Vulnerability Description**  
The code contains an array access outside its valid index range, leading to a runtime exception. Specifically, the loop iterates with a condition that allows the index to reach the array's length, which is invalid in zero-based indexing. This results in an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, which is a manifestation of improper boundary restriction, aligning with CWE-119.

---

**2) Vulnerable Code**  
```java
public class BufferOverflowExample3 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] numbers = new int[5];

        for (int i = 0; i <= numbers.length; i++) { // Incorrect boundary condition
            numbers[i] = i * 10; // Potential ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
        }
    }
}
```

---

**3) Root Cause**  
The loop uses the condition `i <= numbers.length`, which allows `i` to reach `numbers.length` (value 5), exceeding the valid index range `[0..4]`. Java arrays are zero-indexed, and valid indices end at `length - 1`. The correct condition should be `i < numbers.length` to prevent buffer overflows.

---

**4) Impact**  
When the code runs, it will throw an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` during the iteration when `i` equals 5. In a different context or language with manual memory management, such improper boundary checks could lead to memory corruption, data leaks, or security vulnerabilities such as code execution hijacking. In Java, it primarily causes runtime crashes, reducing application stability and reliability.

---

**5) Mitigation**  
- Always use `<` instead of `<=` when iterating over array indices:  
  ```java
  for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) { ... }
  ```
- Incorporate boundary checks or assertions if array bounds are dynamic.
- Utilize enhanced for-loops where applicable, which handle boundaries automatically:  
  ```java
  for (int num : numbers) { ... }
  ```
- Implement static code analysis and testing to detect such boundary violations early during development.

---

**Summary**: The core issue is an incorrect loop boundary condition leading to attempts to access array elements outside valid indices, causing runtime exceptions and potential vulnerabilities. Correct iteration bounds are essential to safeguard against buffer overflows and ensure program stability.

page_content:
**Functionality:**  
Initialize a fixed-size array with two string values and assign a large string to the third element without verifying the array's capacity, demonstrating how improper size management can lead to runtime exceptions or logical errors.

KeyConcept: ArrayBoundsCheckingMistake—This vulnerability arises when code assumes an array or buffer has sufficient capacity for certain operations without explicitly verifying its size beforehand. Such assumptions can lead to attempts to write beyond the allocated boundary of the data structure. In memory-safe environments, this often results in runtime exceptions or errors; in lower-level languages, it can cause memory corruption, crashes, or security breaches. The core issue involves relying on implicit guarantees about data structure size rather than validating or managing the capacity explicitly, creating opportunities for overflow if those guarantees are broken or assumptions are invalidated. Recognizing this pattern is crucial for detecting potential buffer overflow vulnerabilities across various programming languages, especially when handling dynamic or external input data.

**Functionality:**  
Initialize a fixed-size array with two string values and assign a large string to the third element without verifying the array's capacity, demonstrating how improper size management can lead to runtime exceptions or logical errors.
metadata.root_cause: KeyConcept: ArrayBoundsCheckingMistake—This vulnerability arises when code assumes an array or buffer has sufficient capacity for certain operations without explicitly verifying its size beforehand. Such assumptions can lead to attempts to write beyond the allocated boundary of the data structure. In memory-safe environments, this often results in runtime exceptions or errors; in lower-level languages, it can cause memory corruption, crashes, or security breaches. The core issue involves relying on implicit guarantees about data structure size rather than validating or managing the capacity explicitly, creating opportunities for overflow if those guarantees are broken or assumptions are invalidated. Recognizing this pattern is crucial for detecting potential buffer overflow vulnerabilities across various programming languages, especially when handling dynamic or external input data.

page_content:
Functionality:
Extract a substring from a complete message and copy it into a fixed-size character buffer, then display the contents of the buffer.

KeyConcept: Improper boundary validation in data copying operations (such as substrings and array assignments) leads to attempts to access or write beyond allocated memory or data structure limits. This occurs when the code extracts or processes data segments that exceed the size constraints of target buffers without verifying the lengths beforehand. Such lack of validation can cause runtime exceptions or undefined behavior, as operations attempt to read or write outside the intended boundaries. Ensuring that data segments are explicitly constrained to the size of the destination buffer prior to copying or processing is essential to prevent out-of-bounds access, thus maintaining robustness and preventing vulnerabilities related to buffer overflows or memory corruption.

metadata.mitigation:
Phase(s)
Mitigation



Requirements



Strategy: Language Selection


Use a language that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
For example, many languages that perform their own memory management, such as Java and Perl, are not subject to buffer overflows. Other languages, such as Ada and C#, typically provide overflow protection, but the protection can be disabled by the programmer.
Be wary that a language's interface to native code may still be subject to overflows, even if the language itself is theoretically safe.





Architecture and Design



Strategy: Libraries or Frameworks


Use a vetted library or framework that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
Examples include the Safe C String Library (SafeStr) by Messier and Viega [REF-57], and the Strsafe.h library from Microsoft [REF-56]. These libraries provide safer versions of overflow-prone string-handling functions.

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since many buffer overflows are not related to strings.




Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Use automatic buffer overflow detection mechanisms that are offered by certain compilers or compiler extensions. Examples include: the Microsoft Visual Studio /GS flag, Fedora/Red Hat FORTIFY_SOURCE GCC flag, StackGuard, and ProPolice, which provide various mechanisms including canary-based detection and range/index checking. 
 D3-SFCV (Stack Frame Canary Validation) from D3FEND [REF-1334] discusses canary-based detection in detail. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 

 This is not necessarily a complete solution, since these mechanisms only detect certain types of overflows. In addition, the result is still a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application. 





Implementation



Consider adhering to the following rules when allocating and managing an application's memory:

Double check that the buffer is as large as specified.
When using functions that accept a number of bytes to copy, such as strncpy(), be aware that if the destination buffer size is equal to the source buffer size, it may not NULL-terminate the string.
Check buffer boundaries if accessing the buffer in a loop and make sure there is no danger of writing past the allocated space.
If necessary, truncate all input strings to a reasonable length before passing them to the copy and concatenation functions.






Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Run or compile the software using features or extensions that randomly arrange the positions of a program's executable and libraries in memory. Because this makes the addresses unpredictable, it can prevent an attacker from reliably jumping to exploitable code. 
 Examples include Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) [REF-58] [REF-60] and Position-Independent Executables (PIE) [REF-64]. Imported modules may be similarly realigned if their default memory addresses conflict with other modules, in a process known as "rebasing" (for Windows) and "prelinking" (for Linux) [REF-1332] using randomly generated addresses. ASLR for libraries cannot be used in conjunction with prelink since it would require relocating the libraries at run-time, defeating the whole purpose of prelinking. 
 For more information on these techniques see D3-SAOR (Segment Address Offset Randomization) from D3FEND [REF-1335]. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
These techniques do not provide a complete solution.  For instance, exploits frequently use a bug that discloses memory addresses in order to maximize reliability of code execution [REF-1337]. It has also been shown that a side-channel attack can bypass ASLR [REF-1333]




Operation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


 Use a CPU and operating system that offers Data Execution Protection (using hardware NX or XD bits) or the equivalent techniques that simulate this feature in software, such as PaX [REF-60] [REF-61]. These techniques ensure that any instruction executed is exclusively at a memory address that is part of the code segment.  
 For more information on these techniques see D3-PSEP (Process Segment Execution Prevention) from D3FEND [REF-1336]. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since buffer overflows could be used to overwrite nearby variables to modify the software's state in dangerous ways. In addition, it cannot be used in cases in which self-modifying code is required. Finally, an attack could still cause a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application. 




Implementation


Replace unbounded copy functions with analogous functions that support length arguments, such as strcpy with strncpy. Create these if they are not available.

Effectiveness: Moderate

Note: 
This approach is still susceptible to calculation errors, including issues such as off-by-one errors (CWE-193) and incorrectly calculating buffer lengths (CWE-131).

}return dst_buf;

// range of values for the array

CWE-119: Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer






The product performs operations on a memory buffer, but it reads from or writes to a memory location outside the buffer's intended boundary. This may result in read or write operations on unexpected memory locations that could be linked to other variables, data structures, or internal program data.









 





Phase(s)
Mitigation



Requirements

Use a language that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
For example, many languages that perform their own memory management, such as Java and Perl, are not subject to buffer overflows. Other languages, such as Ada and C#, typically provide overflow protection, but the protection can be disabled by the programmer.
Be wary that a language's interface to native code may still be subject to overflows, even if the language itself is theoretically safe.





Architecture and Design



Strategy: Libraries or Frameworks


Use a vetted library or framework that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
Examples include the Safe C String Library (SafeStr) by Messier and Viega [REF-57], and the Strsafe.h library from Microsoft [REF-56]. These libraries provide safer versions of overflow-prone string-handling functions.

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since many buffer overflows are not related to strings.




Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Use automatic buffer overflow detection mechanisms that are offered by certain compilers or compiler extensions. Examples include: the Microsoft Visual Studio /GS flag, Fedora/Red Hat FORTIFY_SOURCE GCC flag, StackGuard, and ProPolice, which provide various mechanisms including canary-based detection and range/index checking. 
 D3-SFCV (Stack Frame Canary Validation) from D3FEND [REF-1334] discusses canary-based detection in detail. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

 This is not necessarily a complete solution, since these mechanisms only detect certain types of overflows. In addition, the result is still a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application.

Replace unbounded copy functions with analogous functions that support length arguments, such as strcpy with strncpy. Create these if they are not available.

struct hostent *hp;in_addr_t *addr;char hostname[64];in_addr_t inet_addr(const char *cp);

/*routine that ensures user_supplied_addr is in the right format for conversion */

...

metadata.report:
**Vulnerability Report**

---

### 1) Vulnerability Description
The code contains a buffer overflow vulnerability due to copying variable-length input into a fixed-size buffer without proper boundary checks. This can lead to unexpected behavior, data corruption, or runtime exceptions.

---

### 2) Vulnerable Code
```java
public class BufferOverflowExample6 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        byte[] buffer = new byte[6];
        String input = "LongInputString";

        // No length check, overwrites buffer
        System.arraycopy(input.getBytes(), 0, buffer, 0, input.length()); // risk of overflow
        System.out.println(new String(buffer));
    }
}
```

---

### 3) Root Cause
The root cause is the use of `System.arraycopy()` with `input.length()` as the length parameter, which exceeds the size of the destination buffer (`6`). Since no bounds check is performed, this leads to an attempt to copy more bytes than the buffer can hold, causing buffer overflow and undefined behavior.

---

### 4) Impact
- **Data Corruption:** Overwrites adjacent memory, corrupting data.
- **Program Crash:** May cause runtime exceptions (e.g., `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`).
- **Security Risks:** Potential exploitation to execute arbitrary code or cause denial of service by crashing the application.

---

### 5) Mitigation
- Always ensure the copy length does not exceed the buffer size:
```java
int lengthToCopy = Math.min(input.length(), buffer.length);
System.arraycopy(input.getBytes(), 0, buffer, 0, lengthToCopy);
```
- Alternatively, validate input length before copying.
- Use higher-level safe APIs or data structures that handle boundary checks automatically.
- Implement proper input validation to restrict input size before processing.

---

page_content:
Functionality:  
Read a chunk of data from standard input into a fixed-size buffer and display the read data as a string, without verifying the actual number of bytes read or handling incomplete input scenarios.

KeyConcept: Improper handling of function return values that indicate the amount of data read from an input stream can lead to logic errors. When reading data into a buffer, the function may return fewer bytes than requested, or indicate end-of-stream, but if the program assumes a full read without validating this return value, it may process incomplete or invalid data. This lack of validation can cause incorrect behavior, data misinterpretation, or runtime exceptions, especially when subsequent operations depend on the completeness and correctness of the input data. Proper validation involves checking whether the read operation returned the expected number of bytes or whether the end of stream has been reached, and handling such cases appropriately to ensure data integrity and correct program logic.

metadata.root_cause: KeyConcept: Improper handling of function return values that indicate the amount of data read from an input stream can lead to logic errors. KeyConcept: ArrayIndexBoundsViolation occurs when code accesses an array element at an index outside the valid range, which spans from zero up to but not including the array's length. metadata.mitigation:
Phase(s)
Mitigation



Requirements



Strategy: Language Selection


Use a language that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
For example, many languages that perform their own memory management, such as Java and Perl, are not subject to buffer overflows. Other languages, such as Ada and C#, typically provide overflow protection, but the protection can be disabled by the programmer.
Be wary that a language's interface to native code may still be subject to overflows, even if the language itself is theoretically safe.





Architecture and Design



Strategy: Libraries or Frameworks


Use a vetted library or framework that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
Examples include the Safe C String Library (SafeStr) by Messier and Viega [REF-57], and the Strsafe.h library from Microsoft [REF-56]. These libraries provide safer versions of overflow-prone string-handling functions.

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since many buffer overflows are not related to strings.




Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Use automatic buffer overflow detection mechanisms that are offered by certain compilers or compiler extensions. Examples include: the Microsoft Visual Studio /GS flag, Fedora/Red Hat FORTIFY_SOURCE GCC flag, StackGuard, and ProPolice, which provide various mechanisms including canary-based detection and range/index checking. 
 D3-SFCV (Stack Frame Canary Validation) from D3FEND [REF-1334] discusses canary-based detection in detail. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 

 This is not necessarily a complete solution, since these mechanisms only detect certain types of overflows. In addition, the result is still a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application. 





Implementation



Consider adhering to the following rules when allocating and managing an application's memory:

Double check that the buffer is as large as specified.
When using functions that accept a number of bytes to copy, such as strncpy(), be aware that if the destination buffer size is equal to the source buffer size, it may not NULL-terminate the string.
Check buffer boundaries if accessing the buffer in a loop and make sure there is no danger of writing past the allocated space.
If necessary, truncate all input strings to a reasonable length before passing them to the copy and concatenation functions.






Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Run or compile the software using features or extensions that randomly arrange the positions of a program's executable and libraries in memory. Because this makes the addresses unpredictable, it can prevent an attacker from reliably jumping to exploitable code. 
 Examples include Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) [REF-58] [REF-60] and Position-Independent Executables (PIE) [REF-64]. Imported modules may be similarly realigned if their default memory addresses conflict with other modules, in a process known as "rebasing" (for Windows) and "prelinking" (for Linux) [REF-1332] using randomly generated addresses. ASLR for libraries cannot be used in conjunction with prelink since it would require relocating the libraries at run-time, defeating the whole purpose of prelinking. 
 For more information on these techniques see D3-SAOR (Segment Address Offset Randomization) from D3FEND [REF-1335]. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
These techniques do not provide a complete solution.  For instance, exploits frequently use a bug that discloses memory addresses in order to maximize reliability of code execution [REF-1337]. It has also been shown that a side-channel attack can bypass ASLR [REF-1333]




Operation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


 Use a CPU and operating system that offers Data Execution Protection (using hardware NX or XD bits) or the equivalent techniques that simulate this feature in software, such as PaX [REF-60] [REF-61]. These techniques ensure that any instruction executed is exclusively at a memory address that is part of the code segment.  
 For more information on these techniques see D3-PSEP (Process Segment Execution Prevention) from D3FEND [REF-1336]. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since buffer overflows could be used to overwrite nearby variables to modify the software's state in dangerous ways. In addition, it cannot be used in cases in which self-modifying code is required. Finally, an attack could still cause a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application. 




Implementation


Replace unbounded copy functions with analogous functions that support length arguments, such as strcpy with strncpy. Create these if they are not available.

Effectiveness: Moderate

Note: 
This approach is still susceptible to calculation errors, including issues such as off-by-one errors (CWE-193) and incorrectly calculating buffer lengths (CWE-131).

metadata.report:
Vulnerability Report

1. Vulnerability Description
The code contains an array index out-of-bounds error caused by an incorrect loop boundary condition. This can lead to runtime exceptions or undefined behavior due to attempts to access memory beyond the array's allocated bounds, aligning with CWE-119: Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer.

2. Vulnerable Code
```java
public class BufferOverflowExample8 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] buffer = new int[3];

        for (int i = 0; i <= buffer.length; i++) { // Incorrect boundary: should be '<' instead of '<='
            buffer[i] = i * 2; // Potential out-of-bounds access when i == buffer.length
        }
    }
}
```

3. Root Cause
The loop condition uses `i <= buffer.length`, which allows `i` to reach `buffer.length`. Since Java array indices are 0-based and valid indices go up to `buffer.length - 1`, this causes an attempt to access `buffer[3]` when `i == 3`, exceeding array bounds and leading to an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

4. Impact
Executing this code results in a runtime exception:

```
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3
    at BufferOverflowExample8.main(BufferOverflowExample8.java:6)
```

This disrupts program execution and may cause application crashes or unpredictable behavior, especially if such errors are unchecked in larger systems.

5. Mitigation
- Correct the loop boundary condition to `i < buffer.length` to ensure index stays within valid bounds.
- Utilize language features or tools (like static analyzers) that detect array boundary violations.
- Implement proper bounds checking if array indices are dynamically computed or manipulated.
- Always test loop boundaries thoroughly to prevent off-by-one errors.

Functionality: Concatenate a fixed prefix string with user-provided input without imposing any size restrictions, resulting in a combined string that displays the combined content.

KeyConcept: Uncontrolled concatenation of unvalidated, potentially large input data into dynamically managed string structures can lead to excessive memory consumption. Although high-level languages employ automatic memory management and do not suffer from traditional buffer overflows, failing to impose size limits or validation on input data can result in resource exhaustion. This may cause application slowdown, out-of-memory errors, or crashes, especially in environments with constrained resources. The core vulnerability arises from the lack of input size checks prior to concatenation, allowing unbounded growth of data stored in memory, which can mimic buffer overflow scenarios by destabilizing application stability and responsiveness.

This may result in read or write operations on unexpected memory locations that could be linked to other variables, data structures, or internal program data.









 
Potential Mitigation: 





Phase(s)
Mitigation



Requirements



Strategy: Language Selection


Use a language that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
For example, many languages that perform their own memory management, such as Java and Perl, are not subject to buffer overflows. Other languages, such as Ada and C#, typically provide overflow protection, but the protection can be disabled by the programmer.
Be wary that a language's interface to native code may still be subject to overflows, even if the language itself is theoretically safe.





Architecture and Design



Strategy: Libraries or Frameworks


Use a vetted library or framework that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
Examples include the Safe C String Library (SafeStr) by Messier and Viega [REF-57], and the Strsafe.h library from Microsoft [REF-56]. These libraries provide safer versions of overflow-prone string-handling functions.

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since many buffer overflows are not related to strings.




Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Use automatic buffer overflow detection mechanisms that are offered by certain compilers or compiler extensions. Examples include: the Microsoft Visual Studio /GS flag, Fedora/Red Hat FORTIFY_SOURCE GCC flag, StackGuard, and ProPolice, which provide various mechanisms including canary-based detection and range/index checking. 
 D3-SFCV (Stack Frame Canary Validation) from D3FEND [REF-1334] discusses canary-based detection in detail. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 

 This is not necessarily a complete solution, since these mechanisms only detect certain types of overflows. In addition, the result is still a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application. 





Implementation



Consider adhering to the following rules when allocating and managing an application's memory:

Double check that the buffer is as large as specified.
When using functions that accept a number of bytes to copy, such as strncpy(), be aware that if the destination buffer size is equal to the source buffer size, it may not NULL-terminate the string.
Check buffer boundaries if accessing the buffer in a loop and make sure there is no danger of writing past the allocated space.
If necessary, truncate all input strings to a reasonable length before passing them to the copy and concatenation functions.






Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Run or compile the software using features or extensions that randomly arrange the positions of a program's executable and libraries in memory. Because this makes the addresses unpredictable, it can prevent an attacker from reliably jumping to exploitable code. 
 Examples include Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) [REF-58] [REF-60] and Position-Independent Executables (PIE) [REF-64]. Imported modules may be similarly realigned if their default memory addresses conflict with other modules, in a process known as "rebasing" (for Windows) and "prelinking" (for Linux) [REF-1332] using randomly generated addresses. ASLR for libraries cannot be used in conjunction with prelink since it would require relocating the libraries at run-time, defeating the whole purpose of prelinking. 
 For more information on these techniques see D3-SAOR (Segment Address Offset Randomization) from D3FEND [REF-1335]. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
These techniques do not provide a complete solution.  For instance, exploits frequently use a bug that discloses memory addresses in order to maximize reliability of code execution [REF-1337]. It has also been shown that a side-channel attack can bypass ASLR [REF-1333]




Operation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


 Use a CPU and operating system that offers Data Execution Protection (using hardware NX or XD bits) or the equivalent techniques that simulate this feature in software, such as PaX [REF-60] [REF-61]. These techniques ensure that any instruction executed is exclusively at a memory address that is part of the code segment.  
 For more information on these techniques see D3-PSEP (Process Segment Execution Prevention) from D3FEND [REF-1336]. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since buffer overflows could be used to overwrite nearby variables to modify the software's state in dangerous ways. In addition, it cannot be used in cases in which self-modifying code is required. Finally, an attack could still cause a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application. 




Implementation


Replace unbounded copy functions with analogous functions that support length arguments, such as strcpy with strncpy. Create these if they are not available.

Effectiveness: Moderate

Note: 
This approach is still susceptible to calculation errors, including issues such as off-by-one errors (CWE-193) and incorrectly calculating buffer lengths (CWE-131).

This example takes an IP address from a user, verifies that it is well formed and then looks up the hostname and copies it into a buffer.

void host_lookup(char *user_supplied_addr){

char * copy_input(char *user_supplied_string){

if( '&' == user_supplied_string[i] ){dst_buf[dst_index++] = '&';dst_buf[dst_index++] = 'a';dst_buf[dst_index++] = 'm';dst_buf[dst_index++] = 'p';dst_buf[dst_index++] = ';';}else if ('<' == user_supplied_string[i] ){
/* encode to < */

}else dst_buf[dst_index++] = user_supplied_string[i];
}return dst_buf;

The programmer attempts to encode the ampersand character in the user-controlled string, however the length of the string is validated before the encoding procedure is applied. As a result, when the encoding procedure expands the string it is possible to overflow the destination buffer if the attacker provides a string of many ampersands.

The following example asks a user for an offset into an array to select an item.




(bad code)

(bad code)

int getValueFromArray(int *array, int len, int index) {

// check that the array index is less than the maximum


// length of the array

(good code)

...

// check that the array index is within the correct


// range of values for the array
if (index >= 0 && index < len) {
...







Example 5

metadata.functionality: Functionality: Concatenate a fixed prefix string with user-provided input without imposing any size restrictions, resulting in a combined string that displays the combined content.
metadata.root_cause: KeyConcept: Uncontrolled concatenation of unvalidated, potentially large input data into dynamically managed string structures can lead to excessive memory consumption. Although high-level languages employ automatic memory management and do not suffer from traditional buffer overflows, failing to impose size limits or validation on input data can result in resource exhaustion. This may cause application slowdown, out-of-memory errors, or crashes, especially in environments with constrained resources. The core vulnerability arises from the lack of input size checks prior to concatenation, allowing unbounded growth of data stored in memory, which can mimic buffer overflow scenarios by destabilizing application stability and responsiveness.

page_content:
Functionality:
Accepts a numeric input from the user via command-line arguments, interprets it as an array index, and assigns a fixed value to the element at that index in the array. It then outputs the value stored at that position in the array.

KeyConcept: [Unvalidated Input Leading to Out-of-Bounds Access] The fundamental mechanism underlying this vulnerability involves using externally provided data, such as user input or external parameters, directly as an index for array or collection access without verifying that the input falls within the valid range of indices. Arrays and similar data structures have defined bounds, typically from zero up to one less than their length. If these bounds are not enforced through explicit validation—by checking that the input index is greater than or equal to zero and less than the length of the data structure—the program can attempt to access memory outside the allocated boundaries. This improper access can cause runtime exceptions, such as index out-of-range errors, which may lead to program crashes, degraded availability, or potentially exploitable states in lower-level languages. Ensuring robust validation of all external inputs used as indices is essential to prevent such vulnerabilities across various programming contexts.

As a result, when the encoding procedure expands the string it is possible to overflow the destination buffer if the attacker provides a string of many ampersands.

// check that the array index is less than the maximum

...

// check that the array index is within the correct

if (index >= 0 && index < len) {
...







Example 5

Functionality:
Accepts a numeric input from the user via command-line arguments, interprets it as an array index, and assigns a fixed value to the element at that index in the array. It then outputs the value stored at that position in the array.
metadata.root_cause: KeyConcept: [Unvalidated Input Leading to Out-of-Bounds Access] The fundamental mechanism underlying this vulnerability involves using externally provided data, such as user input or external parameters, directly as an index for array or collection access without verifying that the input falls within the valid range of indices. Arrays and similar data structures have defined bounds, typically from zero up to one less than their length. If these bounds are not enforced through explicit validation—by checking that the input index is greater than or equal to zero and less than the length of the data structure—the program can attempt to access memory outside the allocated boundaries. This improper access can cause runtime exceptions, such as index out-of-range errors, which may lead to program crashes, degraded availability, or potentially exploitable states in lower-level languages. Ensuring robust validation of all external inputs used as indices is essential to prevent such vulnerabilities across various programming contexts.

page_content:
**Functionality:**  
Limit the number of items added to the shopping cart to ensure the quantity does not exceed the maximum allowed, thereby controlling inventory and preventing excessive additions.

KeyConcept: Range checks on numeric inputs should verify both the minimum and maximum bounds to ensure inputs fall within an expected valid interval. Neglecting to validate the lower boundary allows negative or zero values to pass through, potentially leading to logical errors, data corruption, or security vulnerabilities. Proper validation involves implementing inclusive checks that confirm the input exceeds or equals the minimum threshold and does not surpass the maximum threshold, thereby maintaining data integrity and preventing exploitation through invalid input values.

metadata.title: CWE-839: Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check
metadata.description:
The product checks a value to ensure that it is less than or equal to a maximum, but it does not also verify that the value is greater than or equal to the minimum.

 


Some products use signed integers or floats even when their values are only expected to be positive or 0. An input validation check might assume that the value is positive, and only check for the maximum value. If the value is negative, but the code assumes that the value is positive, this can produce an error. The error may have security consequences if the negative value is used for memory allocation, array access, buffer access, etc. Ultimately, the error could lead to a buffer overflow or other type of memory corruption.
The use of a negative number in a positive-only context could have security implications for other types of resources. For example, a shopping cart might check that the user is not requesting more than 10 items, but a request for -3 items could cause the application to calculate a negative price and credit the attacker's account.
metadata.mitigation:
Phase(s)
Mitigation



Implementation



Strategy: Enforcement by Conversion

If the number to be used is always expected to be positive, change the variable type from signed to unsigned or size_t.




Implementation



Strategy: Input Validation

If the number to be used could have a negative value based on the specification (thus requiring a signed value), but the number should only be positive to preserve code correctness, then include a check to ensure that the value is positive.

Functionality:  
Verify if the requested number of seats does not exceed the maximum allowed limit to authorize a reservation.

KeyConcept:InputValidation: When processing numerical input values that are subject to constraints such as upper and lower bounds, failing to validate that inputs meet all necessary conditions—particularly ensuring that values are within acceptable positive ranges—can lead to acceptance of invalid or nonsensical data. Specifically, checking only for upper limits without verifying that the input is above a minimum threshold (such as zero) allows undesirable values like zero or negative numbers to pass validation. This oversight can cause logical inconsistencies, enable misuse or malicious exploitation, and compromise system integrity. Therefore, comprehensive input validation must include checks for both lower and upper bounds to ensure that only valid and meaningful data is processed.

metadata.report:
**Vulnerability Report**

---

**1) Vulnerability Description**  
The method `reduceStock` permits reduction of stock only if the input `quantityToRemove` is less than or equal to a fixed maximum limit (`maxReduction = 100`). However, it does not enforce a minimum value check or handle negative inputs. This can lead to unintended consequences such as decreasing stock by a negative number, effectively increasing stock, which can cause inconsistent inventory data and potential exploitation.

---

**2) Vulnerable Code**
```java
// 6. Product stock adjustment (only maximum reduction)
public void reduceStock(int quantityToRemove) {
    int maxReduction = 100;
    if (quantityToRemove <= maxReduction) {
        stock -= quantityToRemove;
    }
}
```

---

**3) Root Cause**  
The code compares the input `quantityToRemove` only against an upper bound (`maxReduction`) without validating that it is within a valid, non-negative range. This neglect allows for negative inputs, which, when subtracted from stock, increase the inventory count. The violation aligns with CWE-839: "Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check," because it only considers the maximum permissible value and not the minimum, leading to improper validation of inputs.

---

**4) Impact**  
- **Data Integrity Risk:** Negative inputs can cause stock levels to increase unexpectedly, corrupting inventory data.  
- **Potential Exploitation:** Malicious actors or errors could exploit this flaw to artificially inflate stock, hide theft, or cause discrepancies.  
- **Operational Issues:** Incorrect stock levels may lead to stockouts or oversupply, affecting business operations.

---

**5) Mitigation**  
- Enforce explicit validation to ensure `quantityToRemove` is within a valid range, including a minimum value (e.g., >= 0).  
- Modify the condition to check both lower and upper bounds:
```java
if (quantityToRemove >= 0 && quantityToRemove <= maxReduction) {
    stock -= quantityToRemove;
}
```
- Add error handling for invalid inputs to prevent unintended modifications.  
- Implement comprehensive input validation at the calling site or through validation functions.

metadata.title: CWE-839: Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check
metadata.description:
The product checks a value to ensure that it is less than or equal to a maximum, but it does not also verify that the value is greater than or equal to the minimum.

 


Some products use signed integers or floats even when their values are only expected to be positive or 0. An input validation check might assume that the value is positive, and only check for the maximum value. If the value is negative, but the code assumes that the value is positive, this can produce an error. The error may have security consequences if the negative value is used for memory allocation, array access, buffer access, etc. Ultimately, the error could lead to a buffer overflow or other type of memory corruption.
The use of a negative number in a positive-only context could have security implications for other types of resources. For example, a shopping cart might check that the user is not requesting more than 10 items, but a request for -3 items could cause the application to calculate a negative price and credit the attacker's account.

metadata.report:
Vulnerability Report: CWE-839 - Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check

---

**1) Vulnerability Description**  
The code performs a temperature check to restrict input values to a maximum threshold but lacks validation for minimum bounds. This omission can lead to unexpected or unsafe behavior if the temperature value is below an acceptable lower limit, potentially resulting in incorrect device operation or erroneous data processing.

---

**2) Vulnerable Code**  
```java
// 7. Temperature threshold check in IoT device (only upper bound)
public void setTemperature(int temperatureCelsius) {
    int maxTemperature = 100;
    if (temperatureCelsius <= maxTemperature) {
        this.temperature = temperatureCelsius;
    }
}
```

---

**3) Root Cause**  
The method compares the input temperature only against an upper threshold (`maxTemperature`) without validating if the temperature is above a minimum acceptable limit. Consequently, values below the lower bound (e.g., negative temperatures) are accepted, potentially leading to invalid or unsafe states.

---

**4) Impact**  
- *Data Integrity:* Accepting invalid temperature readings can corrupt stored data.  
- *Device Safety:* Operating with unrealistic or invalid temperatures might cause hardware malfunctions or safety hazards.  
- *Security Risks:* Malicious inputs intentionally set to invalid ranges could cause resource exhaustion or logic errors.

---

**5) Mitigation**  
- Define and enforce both minimum and maximum acceptable temperature bounds.  
- Modify the validation logic to include a lower bound check, such as:  
```java
public void setTemperature(int temperatureCelsius) {
    int minTemperature = -50; // example lower limit
    int maxTemperature = 100; // upper limit
    if (temperatureCelsius >= minTemperature && temperatureCelsius <= maxTemperature) {
        this.temperature = temperatureCelsius;
    }
}
```  
- Implement comprehensive validation and error handling to manage out-of-range inputs appropriately.  
- Regularly review and update acceptable ranges based on device specifications and safety standards.

---

**Summary:**  
To prevent CWE-839 vulnerabilities, validation must encompass the full acceptable data range, including both minimum and maximum bounds, ensuring only valid and safe temperature values are accepted.

metadata.report:
Vulnerability Report: CWE-192: Integer Coercion Error

---

### 1) Vulnerability Description
The code performs an implicit cast from a `long` value to an `int`, which can lead to integer overflow. When the `long` value exceeds the maximum value representable by an `int`, the cast results in data corruption, causing incorrect stock counts that can affect inventory accuracy and system reliability.

---

### 2) Vulnerable Code
```java
public class InventoryChecker {
    public void checkStock() {
        long stockCount = 3000000000L; // large number exceeding int max
        int stock = (int) stockCount; // potential overflow
        System.out.println("Stock count: " + stock);
    }
}
```

---

### 3) Root Cause
The core issue is the explicit casting of a large `long` value (`3000000000L`) to an `int`. Since `int` in Java has a maximum value of `2,147,483,647`, casting larger numbers causes wrapping around, resulting in an incorrect, negative, or otherwise invalid value.

---

### 4) Impact
- **Data Integrity:** The actual stock count is misrepresented, which may lead to incorrect inventory decisions.
- **Business Risks:** Overstocking or stockouts due to inaccurate data.
- **System Reliability:** Potential for cascading errors in inventory calculations, affecting other system components.
- **Security:** While not directly exploitable for malicious purposes, data corruption can lead to unpredictable system states.

---

### 5) Mitigation
- **Check for Overflow:** Before casting, verify that `long` value fits within `int` range:
  ```java
  if (stockCount >= Integer.MIN_VALUE && stockCount <= Integer.MAX_VALUE) {
      int stock = (int) stockCount;
  } else {
      // Handle error: number out of int range
  }
  ```
- **Use Appropriate Data Types:** Store stock counts in `long` if large values are possible, avoiding casting altogether.
- **Input Validation:** Validate input data to ensure it does not exceed expected ranges.
- **Use Safe Conversion Methods:** Employ utility methods that handle overflows explicitly or throw exceptions when out of bounds.

---

This report aims to highlight the importance of proper data type management to prevent integer coercion errors and preserve data integrity within inventory systems.

If the value exceeds the destination type's bounds, the conversion results in truncation, wrapping, or data loss, leading to incorrect or unintended values. This type of coercion can cause data integrity issues, logical errors, or security vulnerabilities, especially when user-controlled input is involved. Proper validation of input range prior to conversion, or choosing appropriate data types for storage and processing, is essential to prevent such errors and maintain the correctness and security of applications.

page_content:
**Functionality:**  
Check if a given object is an instance of an integer and, if so, cast it to an primitive int type and display its value; otherwise, notify that the object is not an integer.

KeyConcept: The vulnerability arises from relying solely on runtime type checks (such as `instanceof`) to determine if an object can be safely cast to a specific primitive wrapper type (e.g., Integer). If the check passes, an explicit cast is performed, which may still lead to runtime exceptions like `ClassCastException` if the object's actual class does not precisely match the expected type or if maliciously crafted objects mimic the target type. This approach assumes that the verification is sufficient to guarantee safe conversion. However, due to class loader issues, type hijacking, or unconventional object instances, such assumptions can be invalid, leading to unhandled exceptions or inconsistent behavior. The core problem is the inadequate type validation that does not consider alternative numeric types or subclassing, risking improper casting and potential security or stability issues within the application.

page_content:
**Functionality:**  
Calculate the shipping fee based on the weight by applying a multiplier, then convert the resulting amount into an integer fee value suitable for billing.

KeyConcept: Casting from floating-point types to integer types truncates the fractional part, which can lead to loss of precision and inaccuracies in calculations. When numerical results involving non-integer values are directly converted to integers without appropriate rounding, the resulting value systematically underestimates (or potentially overestimates) the intended measurement or fee. This truncation can cause financial discrepancies, misbilling, or data integrity issues, especially in applications requiring precise quantification. Recognizing this vulnerability involves understanding that explicit casting does not perform rounding but instead discards fractional components, which can have significant implications in arithmetic operations that involve floating-point calculations.

metadata.report:
Vulnerability Report: CWE-192 - Integer Coercion Error in Shipping Fee Calculation

---

**1) Vulnerability Description**  
The code converts a floating-point calculation result directly to an integer via casting, which can lead to truncation errors. This truncation ignores the fractional part, potentially resulting in undercharged shipping fees. It exposes the system to inaccuracies and possible financial discrepancies.

---

**2) Vulnerable Code**  
```java
public class ShippingFeeCalculator {
    public int calculateFee(double weight) {
        int fee = (int) (weight * 1.5); // possible truncation
        return fee;
    }
}
```

---

**3) Root Cause**  
The root cause is the explicit cast `(int)` of a `double` value resulting from `weight * 1.5`. Since casting truncates the decimal part towards zero, any fractional amount is lost, leading to an underestimation of the fee when floating-point inaccuracy or fractional values are involved.

---

**4) Impact**  
- Underpayment of shipping fees due to truncation.  
- Possible financial loss or revenue leakage.  
- Inaccurate billing that can undermine customer trust or violate accounting standards.  
- Difficulty in auditing or reconciling payments.

---

**5) Mitigation**  
- Use proper rounding methods, such as `Math.round()`, to ensure the fee is rounded correctly to the nearest integer.  
- Example fix:  
  ```java
  int fee = (int) Math.round(weight * 1.5);
  ```  
- Validate input values and consider defining acceptable ranges to prevent unexpected behavior.  
- Implement comprehensive testing with boundary and fractional values to verify correctness.

---

**Summary**  
Replacing direct casting with rounding ensures accurate fee computation, preventing truncation-related vulnerabilities and financial discrepancies.

Functionality: Validate whether the provided input represents an adult's age by accepting either a string or integer input, parsing or casting it as needed, and determining if the age meets the minimum threshold for adulthood.

KeyConcept:type coercion and range validation — Vulnerabilities arise when user-controlled data is converted from one data type to another, such as strings to integers, without sufficient validation of the resulting value's correctness and bounds. If the conversion process relies solely on parsing or casting without enforcing realistic bounds or checking for malformed, negative, or excessively large values, malicious or malformed inputs can lead to incorrect logical outcomes. This may allow inputs that do not accurately represent valid data (e.g., ages outside plausible human ranges or negative values) to pass validation routines, thereby breaching intended access control or data integrity constraints. Proper validation includes not only parsing the input but also verifying that the resulting value falls within a reasonable and predefined acceptable range, preventing exploitation from crafted inputs that exploit assumptions in type conversion logic.

page_content:
Functionality: Accept a control signal value as a 16-bit number, cast it to an 8-bit byte for device communication, and output the resulting control byte, facilitating the transmission of control signals to the device.

KeyConcept: [Type Conversion and Data Truncation within Casting Operations]  
This vulnerability stems from the act of converting a larger numeric data type to a smaller one without validating whether the original value lies within the valid range of the target type. When a wider data type (e.g., a 16-bit integer) is cast to a narrower type (e.g., an 8-bit byte), any value outside the target type’s representable range can either be silently truncated or cause unintended wrapping around. This often results in the original data being altered, which can compromise the correctness of subsequent operations that depend on accurate data representation. Specifically, if validation is not performed prior to casting, significant bits can be lost, leading to erroneous values that may cause misinterpretation, malfunction, or unpredictable behavior in systems relying on precise signal control or data integrity. Recognizing this vulnerability involves understanding that casting operations do not inherently perform range checks, and thus, explicit validation or safeguards are necessary to prevent data loss or unintended consequences across various computational and control scenarios.

Functionality: Access and display an element from a predefined array based on a user-provided index without validating the index, which may result in runtime exceptions or errors if the input is outside the valid array bounds.

Array Index Validation: [This vulnerability occurs when code accesses an array element directly using an index that is provided by external input, without verifying whether this index falls within the valid range of the array's indices. Specifically, arrays have a defined set of valid indices from zero up to the length of the array minus one. If an index outside this range is used, it results in a runtime exception or undefined behavior. This lack of bounds checking can cause application crashes, leading to denial-of-service scenarios, or potentially be exploited to bypass certain security controls if combined with other unsafe operations. Ensuring proper validation involves checking that the external input is greater than or equal to zero and less than the array's length before accessing the element, thereby preventing out-of-bounds access and enhancing robustness.]

metadata.title: CWE-129: Improper Validation of Array Index
metadata.description: The product uses untrusted input when calculating or using an array index, but the product does not validate or incorrectly validates the index to ensure the index references a valid position within the array.
metadata.mitigation:
Phase(s)
Mitigation



Architecture and Design



Strategy: Input Validation

Use an input validation framework such as Struts or the OWASP ESAPI Validation API. Note that using a framework does not automatically address all input validation problems; be mindful of weaknesses that could arise from misusing the framework itself (CWE-1173).




Architecture and Design



For any security checks that are performed on the client side, ensure that these checks are duplicated on the server side, in order to avoid CWE-602. Attackers can bypass the client-side checks by modifying values after the checks have been performed, or by changing the client to remove the client-side checks entirely. Then, these modified values would be submitted to the server.
Even though client-side checks provide minimal benefits with respect to server-side security, they are still useful. First, they can support intrusion detection. If the server receives input that should have been rejected by the client, then it may be an indication of an attack. Second, client-side error-checking can provide helpful feedback to the user about the expectations for valid input. Third, there may be a reduction in server-side processing time for accidental input errors, although this is typically a small savings.





Requirements



Strategy: Language Selection


Use a language that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid.
For example, Ada allows the programmer to constrain the values of a variable and languages such as Java and Ruby will allow the programmer to handle exceptions when an out-of-bounds index is accessed.





Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Run or compile the software using features or extensions that randomly arrange the positions of a program's executable and libraries in memory. Because this makes the addresses unpredictable, it can prevent an attacker from reliably jumping to exploitable code. 
 Examples include Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) [REF-58] [REF-60] and Position-Independent Executables (PIE) [REF-64]. Imported modules may be similarly realigned if their default memory addresses conflict with other modules, in a process known as "rebasing" (for Windows) and "prelinking" (for Linux) [REF-1332] using randomly generated addresses. ASLR for libraries cannot be used in conjunction with prelink since it would require relocating the libraries at run-time, defeating the whole purpose of prelinking. 
 For more information on these techniques see D3-SAOR (Segment Address Offset Randomization) from D3FEND [REF-1335].  

Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
These techniques do not provide a complete solution.  For instance, exploits frequently use a bug that discloses memory addresses in order to maximize reliability of code execution [REF-1337]. It has also been shown that a side-channel attack can bypass ASLR [REF-1333]




Operation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


 Use a CPU and operating system that offers Data Execution Protection (using hardware NX or XD bits) or the equivalent techniques that simulate this feature in software, such as PaX [REF-60] [REF-61]. These techniques ensure that any instruction executed is exclusively at a memory address that is part of the code segment.  
 For more information on these techniques see D3-PSEP (Process Segment Execution Prevention) from D3FEND [REF-1336]. 


Effectiveness: Defense in Depth

Note: 
This is not a complete solution, since buffer overflows could be used to overwrite nearby variables to modify the software's state in dangerous ways. In addition, it cannot be used in cases in which self-modifying code is required. Finally, an attack could still cause a denial of service, since the typical response is to exit the application. 




Implementation



Strategy: Input Validation


Assume all input is malicious. Use an "accept known good" input validation strategy, i.e., use a list of acceptable inputs that strictly conform to specifications. Reject any input that does not strictly conform to specifications, or transform it into something that does.
When performing input validation, consider all potentially relevant properties, including length, type of input, the full range of acceptable values, missing or extra inputs, syntax, consistency across related fields, and conformance to business rules. As an example of business rule logic, "boat" may be syntactically valid because it only contains alphanumeric characters, but it is not valid if the input is only expected to contain colors such as "red" or "blue."
Do not rely exclusively on looking for malicious or malformed inputs.  This is likely to miss at least one undesirable input, especially if the code's environment changes. This can give attackers enough room to bypass the intended validation. However, denylists can be useful for detecting potential attacks or determining which inputs are so malformed that they should be rejected outright.
When accessing a user-controlled array index, use a stringent range of values that are within the target array. Make sure that you do not allow negative values to be used. That is, verify the minimum as well as the maximum of the range of acceptable values.





Implementation


Be especially careful to validate all input when invoking code that crosses language boundaries, such as from an interpreted language to native code. This could create an unexpected interaction between the language boundaries. Ensure that you are not violating any of the expectations of the language with which you are interfacing. For example, even though Java may not be susceptible to buffer overflows, providing a large argument in a call to native code might trigger an overflow.




Architecture and Design; Operation



Strategy: Environment Hardening

Run your code using the lowest privileges that are required to accomplish the necessary tasks [REF-76]. If possible, create isolated accounts with limited privileges that are only used for a single task. That way, a successful attack will not immediately give the attacker access to the rest of the software or its environment. For example, database applications rarely need to run as the database administrator, especially in day-to-day operations.




Architecture and Design; Operation



Strategy: Sandbox or Jail


Run the code in a "jail" or similar sandbox environment that enforces strict boundaries between the process and the operating system. This may effectively restrict which files can be accessed in a particular directory or which commands can be executed by the software.
OS-level examples include the Unix chroot jail, AppArmor, and SELinux. In general, managed code may provide some protection. For example, java.io.FilePermission in the Java SecurityManager allows the software to specify restrictions on file operations.
This may not be a feasible solution, and it only limits the impact to the operating system; the rest of the application may still be subject to compromise.
Be careful to avoid CWE-243 and other weaknesses related to jails.


Effectiveness: Limited

Note: 
The effectiveness of this mitigation depends on the prevention capabilities of the specific sandbox or jail being used and might only help to reduce the scope of an attack, such as restricting the attacker to certain system calls or limiting the portion of the file system that can be accessed.

metadata.functionality: Functionality: Access and display an element from a predefined array based on a user-provided index without validating the index, which may result in runtime exceptions or errors if the input is outside the valid array bounds.
metadata.root_cause: Array Index Validation: [This vulnerability occurs when code accesses an array element directly using an index that is provided by external input, without verifying whether this index falls within the valid range of the array's indices. Specifically, arrays have a defined set of valid indices from zero up to the length of the array minus one. If an index outside this range is used, it results in a runtime exception or undefined behavior. This lack of bounds checking can cause application crashes, leading to denial-of-service scenarios, or potentially be exploited to bypass certain security controls if combined with other unsafe operations. Ensuring proper validation involves checking that the external input is greater than or equal to zero and less than the array's length before accessing the element, thereby preventing out-of-bounds access and enhancing robustness.]

page_content:
Functionality: Accepts a string input representing an index, converts it to an integer, and retrieves the corresponding item from a predefined array without validating whether the index falls within the valid range.

KeyConcept: [Array index validation involves verifying that an index used to access array elements falls within the valid range of indices, typically from zero up to one less than the length of the array. Failure to perform appropriate bounds checking allows for negative or excessively large indices to be used, which can result in runtime exceptions or unintended data access. Such improper validation can lead to application crashes, data corruption, or security vulnerabilities if exploited to access sensitive data or cause denial of service. Ensuring that the index is within acceptable limits before array access mitigates these risks and maintains data integrity and application stability.]

metadata.root_cause: KeyConcept:ArrayIndexValidationIncomplete { The core issue arises when bounds checking for array access permits an index value equal to the array's length, which exceeds the valid index range due to zero-based indexing. Valid indices for arrays are from 0 up to (length - 1). If validation conditions allow the index to be equal to or greater than the length, attempts to access the array will result in runtime exceptions indicating an out-of-bounds access. This vulnerability manifests when input validation logic does not correctly enforce that the index is strictly less than the array's length, leading to potential crashes, unhandled exceptions, or unpredictable behavior. Ensuring proper validation involves confirming that the index is greater than or equal to zero and strictly less than the array's length, thereby maintaining access within legitimate bounds.}

page_content:
Functionality: Access and display a specific value from a predefined array based on user-provided input, treating the input as an index without validation.

KeyConcept: InputValidationArrayIndexing [This vulnerability arises from the failure to validate or sanitize user-supplied input before using it as an index for array access. When external data—often in string form—is directly converted to an integer without proper error handling and then used to access an array, it can lead to out-of-bounds errors or unintended behavior. Specifically, if the input is not a valid number, the parsing process may fail or produce exceptions; if the number is outside the valid index range of the array, it causes runtime exceptions such as out-of-bounds errors. Such errors can disrupt normal program operation and may be exploited maliciously to cause denial of service, crash the application, or probe system internals. To mitigate this vulnerability, it is essential to verify that the input is a valid integer and that it falls within the permissible index range of the array before performing the access. Proper exception handling and input validation are critical to prevent untrusted data from causing unintended side effects or security issues.]

For any security checks that are performed on the client side, ensure that these checks are duplicated on the server side, in order to avoid CWE-602. Attackers can bypass the client-side checks by modifying values after the checks have been performed, or by changing the client to remove the client-side checks entirely. Then, these modified values would be submitted to the server.

Third, there may be a reduction in server-side processing time for accidental input errors, although this is typically a small savings.

Operation; Build and Compilation



Strategy: Environment Hardening


Run or compile the software using features or extensions that randomly arrange the positions of a program's executable and libraries in memory. Because this makes the addresses unpredictable, it can prevent an attacker from reliably jumping to exploitable code.

Operation

 Use a CPU and operating system that offers Data Execution Protection (using hardware NX or XD bits) or the equivalent techniques that simulate this feature in software, such as PaX [REF-60] [REF-61]. page_content:
**Functionality:**  
Validate an input index and, if valid, access and display the corresponding color from an array; otherwise, inform the user of an invalid index.

KeyConcept:Off-by-one errors occur when boundary checks in array or collection access operations are incorrectly specified, typically allowing an index value that exceeds the maximum valid index. This results in attempts to access elements outside the allocated range, leading to runtime exceptions such as out-of-bounds errors. Such validation flaws compromise program stability and can potentially expose applications to unexpected behaviors, unauthorized data access, or crashes. Accurate boundary validation must precisely match the valid index range, usually from zero up to one less than the total length, ensuring only legitimate indices are permitted for data access.
